title: Review: Human reproduction and gametogenesis; Chromosomes, karyotypes and genome organisation; Sources of genetic variation in meiosis and fertilisation; Meiosis
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: RP01a#t3 term and clue written for the game; CD03#t4 term and clue written for the game; CD04#t1 term and clue written for the game; RP01a#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: CD03#N.3, CD04#N.6, CD05b#N.3, RP01a#N.7, CD03#N.10b, CD04#N.13, RP01a#N.13, RP01a#N.10. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Zona pellucida
items.clue: Glycoprotein layer outside the egg membrane, to which sperm bind.

items.label: Homologous chromosomes
items.clue: A matching maternal and paternal pair with the same genes at the same loci

items.label: Crossing over
items.clue: Exchange of equivalent sections between non-sister chromatids in prophase I

items.label: Midpiece
items.clue: Part of a sperm packed with mitochondria that supply ATP for the flagellum.

questions.stem: A diploid nucleus of an organism with 2n = 14 undergoes meiosis. What is produced?

options.text: Four diploid nuclei, each containing 14 chromosomes
Four haploid nuclei, each with half of the organism's genes
Two haploid nuclei, each containing 7 chromosomes
Four haploid nuclei, each containing 7 chromosomes

questions.explanation: Two divisions give four haploid nuclei from one diploid nucleus. 2n = 14, so each has n = 7: one of each homologous pair.

questions.stem: Which statement describes crossing over during meiosis?

options.text: The two sister chromatids of one chromosome exchange their segments in prophase I.
At a chiasma, all four chromatids of a homologous pair exchange segments in prophase I.
Non-sister chromatids of a homologous pair exchange segments in prophase I.
Homologous pairs swap the sides of the plate they face at metaphase I.

questions.explanation: While homologues are paired in prophase I, non-sister chromatids exchange corresponding segments at chiasmata, making new combinations of alleles.

questions.stem: A person has two different alleles of the ABO blood group gene, which has its locus on chromosome 9. Where are these two alleles in one of the person's body cells?

options.text: One on each chromosome 9 of the homologous pair, at the same locus on each.
Both on the same chromosome 9, side by side at two neighbouring loci.
On chromosome 9, at a locus that varies from one person to another.
Only one allele is in a body cell; the other allele is found only in gametes.

questions.explanation: Homologues carry the same genes at the same loci. One allele came from each parent, on that parent's chromosome 9.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly matches an adaptation of a human gamete to its function?

options.text: Egg cytoplasm with nutrient stores: supplies the embryo's first divisions.
Sperm acrosome: stores the fuel that the mitochondria respire while the sperm swims.
Egg zona pellucida: a cell wall that gives the egg mechanical protection from damage.
Egg and sperm of matching size: each gamete carries half of the chromosomes needed.

questions.explanation: The egg is large because its cytoplasm contains stored nutrients (yolk droplets) that supply the embryo during its first divisions, before it can obtain nutrients from the mother.

questions.stem: Which describes the cells produced when one spermatocyte, a diploid cell in the testis of an animal that is heterozygous for many genes, completes meiosis?

options.text: Two cells, genetically different from each other
Four cells, all genetically identical to one another
Two cells, genetically identical to each other
Four cells, each genetically different from the others

questions.explanation: One diploid cell gives four haploid cells. Each gets one homologue of every pair, and crossing over mixes alleles between chromatids, so in a heterozygous animal the four differ.

questions.stem: A mutation in a hypothetical species of animal prevents crossing over during meiosis, but meiosis is otherwise normal. Compared with the gametes of a normal individual, which prediction about the gametes of an individual with this mutation is correct?

options.text: Every gamete would be genetically identical, since crossing over is the only source of genetic variation.
They would vary less but still differ, because homologous pairs still orient randomly at metaphase I.
They would vary just as much as before, since crossing over just swaps sister chromatid segments.
Each gamete would carry either the full maternal or the full paternal set of chromosomes.

questions.stem: In a fish species the female lays a few hundred large eggs in a nest and the male releases many millions of tiny sperm over them. Which statement explains the difference in size and number?

options.text: Eggs are larger because each one carries far more of the genetic material than a sperm does.
The numbers should be equal since one sperm fertilises one egg; the surplus sperm are defective ones.
Sperm are small because so many are made that only a little cytoplasm is available for each one.
Sperm must travel to the eggs, so they are small with few food reserves and can be produced cheaply in vast numbers.

questions.stem: In an experiment, eggs treated so that they could not carry out the cortical reaction were each entered by several sperm. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Without the cortical reaction the zona pellucida is not hardened, so further sperm can still digest through it and fuse.
The cortical reaction is what lets the first sperm in, so blocking it should have stopped fertilisation altogether.
Sperm bore through the egg membrane with their enzymes, so hardening the zona could not have stopped them.
Only one sperm normally reaches the egg, so the treatment must somehow have attracted extra sperm to it.
